claims.claim: Erosion is the transport of weathered material from one place to another: weathering loosens or alters rock in place, and once the particle is moved by flowing water, wind, or ice, it is erosion.

The main agents of erosion are running water, wind, ice (glaciers), and gravity; sediment is the loose, uncemented rock and mineral material these agents carry, classified by size from boulders through cobbles, pebbles, sand, silt, and clay.

Running water is a major transporting agent: fast-moving water can pick up, suspend, and carry larger particles than slow-moving water, and when flow slows, coarser grains settle first, so water-laid deposits tend to be sorted by grain size.
Wind transports loose, dry particles, mainly sand and silt, in deserts and coastal regions; wind-laid deposits are fine-grained, and windblown sand can pile into dunes where the wind drops its load.

Glacial ice transports everything from clay to boulders mixed together; sediment deposited directly by glacial ice (till) has a wide range of grain sizes and is normally unbedded, so ice does not sort material the way water and wind do.

Mass wasting is the downslope movement of rock and soil under gravity without a flowing medium; creep is imperceptibly slow (millimeters to centimeters per year), slump is rotational sliding of a block along a curved surface in thick unconsolidated deposits (centimeters to meters per year, often with excess water), a rockslide is translational sliding of rock along a roughly planar surface, and a debris flow is a rapid slurry of soil, rock, organic matter, and water moving downslope at meters per second.

Deposition is the accumulation of eroded sediment where transport energy drops; erosion removes material from one place while deposition lays it down elsewhere, and a single stream can erode and deposit at the same time.

Erosion shapes recognizable landforms: running water cuts canyons over long spans of time; wave erosion produces sea cliffs, stacks, and arches along coasts; and erosion of less-resistant rock layers creates natural arches, such as the more than 2,000 documented arches in Arches National Park.

Human activities that remove vegetation or expose bare soil can speed erosion: storms deliver eroded soil and debris to rivers, construction sites without runoff controls add large amounts of suspended sediment that harms water quality, vegetation removal is a recognized cause of slope failure, and concentrated runoff on bare ground cuts channels (gullies) on steep slopes.

The U.S. Geological Survey estimated in 2004 that landslides in the United States cause approximately $3.5 billion (2001 dollars) in damage and kill between 25 and 50 people annually; casualties are primarily caused by rockfalls, rock slides, and debris flows.
On average, dissolved material makes up about 15 percent of the mass a stream transports; the rest moves as solid grains of varying size.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The simple rule that faster water moves larger grains glosses over fine-particle behavior.
positions: USGS Water Science School: fast-moving water can pick up, suspend, and move larger particles more easily than slow-moving water.

Open Textbook BC (Hjulstrom-Sundborg diagram): silt and clay grains stick together and actually require higher velocities to be eroded from a stream bed than medium sand does, even though they settle very slowly once suspended.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps the general rule for transport capacity while avoiding the claim that the smallest grains are always the easiest to erode; the cohesion nuance is noted as a refinement covered in the rivers topic.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Landslide damage and casualty figures are dated estimates.
positions: USGS Fact Sheet 2004-3072: about $3.5 billion (year 2001 dollars) in damage and 25 to 50 deaths per year in the United States.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the figures explicitly to the 2004 USGS estimate rather than presenting them as current statistics.

sourceRecords.title: Landslide Types and Processes
sourceRecords.notes: USGS Fact Sheet 2004-3072 (July 2004), read live. Supports: landslides as downward and outward movement of slope-forming materials by falling, sliding, or flowing; creep as imperceptibly slow, steady downward movement indicated by curved tree trunks and tilted poles; rotational slides (slump-like, curved rupture surface) versus translational slides (rockslide, roughly planar surface); debris flow as a rapid slurry of soil, rock, organic matter, air, and water; vegetation removal as a landslide cause; the 2004 estimate of roughly $3.5 billion (2001 dollars) in annual U.S. landslide damage and 25-50 deaths per year. Reference only.

Reference only.
